power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The sample consisted of 154 individuals organized into 77 dyads. Participants were recruited through student organization email lists and Facebook advertisements and were paired with an interaction partner who was unfamiliar to them at the time. The age range was 18 to 68 years (M = 28.34, SD = 10.60). Of the total sample, 104 participants identified as women and 50 as men. 90 participants (58.44%) were Finnish speaking and 64 (41.56%) were Swedish speaking. The participants were divided into face-to-face (41 dyads, 82 participants) and video-mediated (36 dyads, 72 participants) conditions. Each dyad consisted of two same-gender participants. Table 1 A Monte Carlo simulation-based sensitivity power analysis was conducted to estimate the minimum detectable effect sizes for the regression models (Lakens, 2022). The simulations reproduced the models used in the main analyses, including the observed predictor structure and dyad-clustered CR2 standard errors with Satterthwaite-adjusted degrees of freedom.
table.header: 2.1 Participants

table.text: Sensitivity was estimated separately for the main effects of actor and partner personality traits and for trait × communication medium interactions. To account for dependence between dyad members, outcome-specific residual within-dyad correlations estimated from the observed data were incorporated into the simulations. With 154 participants nested within 77 dyads, α = .05, and 80% power, the minimum detectable standardized actor and partner trait effects ranged from β = 0.23 to 0.28 across traits and outcomes, whereas the minimum detectable trait × medium interaction effects ranged from β = 0.24 to 0.28. Summary data files used in the statistical analyses and all analysis scripts are openly available in a GitHub repository: XX. To protect participants' privacy and comply with applicable data protection requirements and the procedures specified in the study's privacy notice, the content of the conversational transcripts has been masked. For the same reasons, the original video and audio recordings are not publicly available.
table.header: 2.1 Participants

table.text: Finally, although the present sample was relatively large for a dyadic interaction study, statistical power was limited for detecting small personality effects. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the study had 80% power to detect standardized actor and partner effects of approximately β = .23-.28 and trait × medium interaction effects of β = .24-.28, depending on the trait and outcome. Several of the observed personality effects were smaller than these values, suggesting that effects of comparable or smaller magnitude could have remained undetected. This is particularly important when interpreting the results for H2: although the findings indicate that trait effects did not differ substantially between face-to-face and video-mediated interaction, smaller moderating effects of communication medium cannot be ruled out. Larger dyadic samples will therefore be needed to determine whether the communication medium moderates some trait-behavior associations to a smaller degree.
table.header: 5 Limitations and future directions

The participants were separated by a curtain in order to prevent interaction between them before the task.
In the video-mediated condition, participants were escorted to separate rooms.

By the end of the study the curtain was closed for the face-to-face condition, while the Zoom call ended in the video-call condition, after which participants completed a set of personality questionnaires.

The head and torso recordings of each participant were first cut and temporally aligned based on the sound cues marking task onset and offset, and then paired with their dyadic partner's recording into a combined video using Filmora software (Wondershare Technology Co., Ltd.).
All participants gave informed consent prior to participation and received compensation valued at 30 euros following the experiment.

text.text: Little is known about how Big Five personality traits manifest in specific conversational behaviors or whether these associations depend on the communication medium.
We examined 154 individuals interacting with strangers face-to-face or via video.
Using manual annotations, computer vision, and LLMs, we examined actor and partner personality associations with turn-taking dynamics, engagement signalling, and topic development.
Higher actor and partner extraversion predicted faster turn-taking and pronounced engagement signalling, whereas actor openness predicted slower turn-taking and reduced engagement signalling.
In actors, conscientiousness predicted nodding and in partners it predicted broader topic exploration.
However, we found no evidence that these associations differed between face-to-face and video-mediated interaction.
Personality thus shapes conversational behavior and these interactional fingerprints appear to survive technological transmission.
Conversations are the cornerstone of human sociality, through which information is shared, relationships are formed and maintained, and collaboration toward shared goals takes place.
The progression of conversation depends on a remarkable degree of coordination between participants.
Interactants must continuously manage turns of speaking and listening, display their engagement as listeners, and contribute content that advances the conversation (Cooney & Wheatley, 2025).
text.formatted: Interactants must continuously manage turns of speaking and listening, display their engagement as listeners, and contribute content that advances the conversation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cooney & Wheatley, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These processes are reflected in a wide range of verbal and non-verbal processeshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?3uF275 including turn-taking dynamics (Levinson & Torreirahttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?UqMovW 2015; Sacks et al., 1974) , listener behaviors such as vocal backchanneling, gaze shifts, nodding, and smiling (Schegloff, 1982; Stivers, 2008) , and the development of conversational content through the generation, pursuit, and closure of topics (Button & Casey, 1985; Schmidt et al., 2025).

text.text: Together, these behavioral patterns constitute the building blocks through which human sociality manifests and related personality differences emerge.
The idea that personality is manifested in fingerprint patterns of conversational behavior has a long history.

More than five decades ago, Bales (1970) proposed that stable individual differences could be understood through recurring patterns of verbal and non-verbal behavior emerging during social interaction.
text.formatted: More than five decades ago, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bales (1970)</ref> proposed that stable individual differences could be understood through recurring patterns of verbal and non-verbal behavior emerging during social interaction.

text.text: Yet, despite this longstanding interactional perspective on personality, surprisingly few studies have systematically examined how personality traits manifest across the specific conversational processes.

Moreover, as social interaction increasingly takes place across both face-to-face and technology-mediated environments, it remains unclear whether these behavioral manifestations of personality are preserved across communication media (Baumaister et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Moreover, as social interaction increasingly takes place across both face-to-face and technology-mediated environments, it remains unclear whether these behavioral manifestations of personality are preserved across communication media <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baumaister et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The current study builds on this decades-old idea by providing a fine-grained, multimethod examination of how personality is expressed across turn-taking dynamics, listener engagement, and conversational content, and whether these "interactional fingerprints" differ between face-to-face and video-mediated interaction.

A fundamental feature of conversation is the turn-taking system through which interactants coordinate who holds the floor, for how long, and how much time elapses between successive turns (Levinson, 2016; Sacks et al., 1974).

text.text: Because these processes are readily observable, researchers have long quantified turn-taking behavior using measures such as turn count, turn duration, and speech gaps (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?DCPaed  Cassotta et al., 1964; Chapple, 1939).

text.text: Beyond the coordination of speaking turns, conversations also depend on what is being said-that is, on the continuous development of shared content through the introduction, maintenance, and transition of conversational topics (Button & Casey, 1985; Schegloff, 1982).

text.text: Throughout conversation, interactants move through the semantic topic space, creating a common ground and exploring new ideas.

Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) through large language models (LLMs) have made it possible to quantify these semantic trajectories by measuring topic shift strength between consecutive turns and semantic exploration breadth across the entire encounter (Schmidt et al., 2025; Speer et al., 2024).

text.text: To our knowledge, there is only one study that has used this methodological approach to examine personality differences in conversational topic development (Fischer & Ram, 2024).

text.text: The authors examined to what extent differences in interlocutors' personality traits predicted the breadth of topics covered during a conversation and the semantic shift between turns.

They found that especially dyads with different levels of openness explored the topic space more broadly whereas dyads with differing levels of extraversion showed decrease in semantic alignment along conversation.

Yet, the focus on dyad-level effects makes it impossible to make individual-level inferences about actor effects (how individuals' own traits predict their own behavior) and partner effects (how their partners' traits predict their behavior).
It is therefore crucial to examine also the actor and partner effects of Big-Five traits on the development of conversation content.
Yet, conversation involves more than the speaking turns.

While the speaker holds the floor, the listener actively displays engagement through a range of verbal and non-verbal behaviors including turn dynamics, brief vocalizations ("hmm", "oh really?"), nods, gaze shifts, and smiles (Bavelas et al., 2000; Peräkylä et al., 2022; Stivers, 2008).

text.text: Therefore, engagement signalling is a fundamental mechanism through which conversations are maintained.
However, relatively little research has examined how individual differences in personality shape these engagement displays.

Existing studies suggest that especially extraversion, agreeableness, and openness are associated with differences in engagement signalling (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?MKDcix  Berry & Hansen, 2000; Cuperman & Ickes, 2009a; Funder & Sneed, 1993; Huang & Gratch, 2013).

text.text: Thus, there is a need to revisit the association between personality and engagement signalling using modern multimethod approaches in naturalistic social interaction.

The need to understand personality in conversational behavior has become increasingly important following the rapid adoption of video calling across diverse social contexts, ranging from job interviews and medical consultations to dating and workplace meetings.

While this technological transition has brought many benefits, it has also been associated with altered turn-dynamics and reduced engagement between interaction partners compared to face-to-face communication (Boland et al., 2022a; Brucks & Levav, 2022; Söderman et al., 2026).

text.text: Thus, video-mediated communication seems to constrain several key conversational behaviors by hampering associated socio-emotional coordination.
Consequently, the influence of personality on engagement signalling may also differ between face-to-face and video-mediated interaction.

Finally, to examine the extent to which Big Five traits shape conversational behaviors and whether these effects are altered by communication technology, interaction should be observed in a context where these micro-interactional processes, such as speech gaps and nods, play a particularly important role.
One such context is interaction between previously unacquainted interlocutors.
First encounters are characterized by heightened uncertainty and a strong motivation to establish rapport and maintain a positive interactional climate (Flint, 2019; Haugh & Carbaugh, 2015).

text.text: Both individuals' own and their partners' personality traits may shape the introduction, maintenance, and transition of conversational topics across turns, giving rise to variation in the semantic patterns of one's speech content.
Finally, when strangers interact, engagement signalling becomes particularly consequential for the progression of the interaction and mutual affiliation.

Behaviors such as vocal backchanneling, nodding, and smiles not only signify understanding and affiliation but also provide a natural arena through which stable individual differences may be expressed.
Nowadays increasing amounts of consequential first encounters, including first dates, job interviews, and medical appointments, happen through video-calls.

It is therefore important to understand whether the interactional fingerprints of personality emerge similarly across face-to-face and video-mediated interactions, or whether technological mediation alters how personality is expressed in conversation.

In the present study, we examined how general Big Five personality traits influence a wide range of conversational behaviors during first encounters and whether the medium through which the conversation takes place moderates these trait-effects.
Individuals were randomly assigned to one of two communication medium conditions (face-to-face or video call) and were asked to be acquainted with a same-sex stranger.

By focusing on previously unacquainted participants, the design minimizes the influence of shared interactional history while enabling a systematic examination of personality and medium-related differences in three different behavioral processes: turn-taking dynamics, engagement signalling, and content development.

To examine personality-related variation in conversational behavior, the present study focuses on Big Five personality traits: openness to experiences, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism (McCrae & John, 1992).

text.text: The Big Five was selected as the framework for examining personality because it is still the most widely used, empirically validated, and extensively studied model of personality in contemporary psychology (John et al., 2008).

Of the Big Five traits, particularly extraversion, agreeableness, and openness have been previously associated with conversational behavior, as cited above.
At the same time, traits like conscientiousness and neuroticism may also influence how individuals coordinate turns, participate in content development, and display engagement as listeners.

text.text: To capture the multimodal nature of conversational behavior and unilateral contributions of both speaker and listener, we examined three behavior clusters: turn-taking dynamics (turn length, speech gaps between turns), content development (topic exploration breadth across the entire encounter, topic shift strength between turns), and engagement signalling while listening (vocal backchannels, nods, smiles, gaze orientation).
While turn-taking dynamics and content development primarily capture speaker behavior, engagement signalling captures the listener's verbal and nonverbal contributions to the interaction.

Of the content development variables, topic exploration breadth captured how broadly a person explored different topics over time, whereas topic shift strength captured local, turn-to-turn transitions between topics.

To characterize these complementary aspects of conversational behavior, we combined manual annotation of speaking turns, nods, and backchannels with natural language processing (NLP) of content development, and computer-vision-based analysis of listener non-verbal behavior.

The sample consisted of 154 individuals organized into 77 dyads.
Participants were recruited through student organization email lists and Facebook advertisements and were paired with an interaction partner who was unfamiliar to them at the time.
The age range was 18 to 68 years (M = 28.34, SD = 10.60).
Of the total sample, 104 participants identified as women and 50 as men. 90 participants (58.44%) were Finnish speaking and 64 (41.56%) were Swedish speaking.
The participants were divided into face-to-face (41 dyads, 82 participants) and video-mediated (36 dyads, 72 participants) conditions.
Each dyad consisted of two same-gender participants.

With 154 participants nested within 77 dyads, α = .05, and 80% power, the minimum detectable standardized actor and partner trait effects ranged from β = 0.23 to 0.28 across traits and outcomes, whereas the minimum detectable trait × medium interaction effects ranged from β = 0.24 to 0.28.

To protect participants' privacy and comply with applicable data protection requirements and the procedures specified in the study's privacy notice, the content of the conversational transcripts has been masked.
For the same reasons, the original video and audio recordings are not publicly available.
Before the study began, participants were informed about the study protocol and their right to discontinue participation at any time, after which they signed an informed consent form.
The participants were kept separate before the experimental task in order to prevent interaction between them.
In the face-to-face condition, participants were escorted to the same room, into designated chairs.
The participants were separated by a curtain in order to prevent interaction between them before the task.
In the video-mediated condition, participants were escorted to separate rooms.
Participants received individual instructions from diagonally positioned monitors in both settings.

text.text: Illustration of the laboratory setting and the experimental procedure.
Participants used a small keypad to initiate the session and give responses to self-reports according to the instructions displayed on the monitors.
In the video-mediated condition, the participants also had a laptop for the Zoom video call and a microphone headset for auditory communication.
During preparation, the audiovisual recording setup was installed and calibrated.
Audio was captured using chest-mounted microphones.

In the face-to-face condition, both participants' upper bodies were recorded using video cameras positioned diagonally in opposite corners of the room, whereas in the video-call condition, each participant was recorded using a video camera positioned at the corner of their desk.
In both conditions, the camera view was adjusted to capture the same portion of the participants' upper body and face.
After the preparation phase, the curtain separating the participants was removed in the face-to-face condition.
In the video call condition, the Zoom video call was activated at this stage, with the self-view turned off.
Thereafter, the researchers moved behind a curtain and remained out of sight for the duration of the interaction.
Next, the monitors instructed the participants to press the down arrow key to launch the Getting Acquainted task.
Pressing of the key triggered a brief sound signalling the start of the task.
Participants then engaged in a five-minute unstructured, spontaneous conversation, during which they were instructed to introduce themselves and become familiar with their interaction partner.
After five minutes, the monitors displayed the message "Time for getting acquainted has ended," accompanied by a brief sound signalling the end of the task.
The onset and offset sound cues were used to cut and temporally align the audio and video recordings during data processing.

By the end of the study the curtain was closed for the face-to-face condition, while the Zoom call ended in the video-call condition, after which participants completed a set of personality questionnaires.
The E-Prime 3 stimulus presentation software was used to implement the experimental procedure on two separate computers (Lenovo ThinkPad L13 Gen 3 laptops), one for each participant.
The systems were synchronized using a local server connection over Ethernet, which provided a temporally aligned experimental progression.
An adjacent monitor was used to provide instructions to each participant (HP Compaq LA2205wg 22-inch widescreen LCD monitor).

In the video call condition, participants communicated through a secured Zoom video call using the local wireless network of the X. The video and audio signals for the video-mediated communication were captured using Logitech C270 HD webcams (720p resolution) and Logitech Stereo Headset H111, respectively.
Zoom's self-view was disabled in all video-mediated encounters.
Video recordings of the head and torso were captured in both conditions to document the participants' behavior during the task.
In both the face-to-face and video-call conditions, interactions were recorded using Canon Legria HF R88 video cameras.
In the video-call condition, the interaction was additionally recorded using Zoom's built-in recording function, with Logitech C270 HD webcams providing the video feed.
The Zoom recordings were used for subsequent behavioral analysis in the video-call condition because they captured the view of each participant as it was transmitted to their interaction partner.
AKG B29L lavalier microphones were attached to each participant's chest to obtain high-quality audio recordings of the interactions.

The head and torso recordings of each participant were first cut and temporally aligned based on the sound cues marking task onset and offset, and then paired with their dyadic partner's recording into a combined video using Filmora software (Wondershare Technology Co., Ltd.).
After that, the backchanneling behaviors and turn-taking were annotated in ELAN (v.
6.9), which yielded 27 531 annotated instances.
Only the first five minutes of interaction (the duration of the Getting Acquainted task) were annotated, aiming for comparability between dyads.
For each participant, vocal backchannels and head nods were coded on different annotation tiers by two trained coders.
All behavioral elements (turns, vocal backchannels, and nods) within any given dyad were coded by a single annotator.

Each coder's annotations for their first dyad were reviewed by a researcher with training in conversation-analytical transcription to ensure consistency with the coding criteria (see Measures for inter-rater reliability analysis).
The onset and offset times of each turn and vocal backchannel were marked using the audible onset and offset of the instance, informed by the audio waveform.

Turns were annotated following the framework of Sacks et al. (1974), according to which speech is organized into turn-constructional units (TCUs) that project possible completion points, or transition-relevance places (TRPs).

text.text: A new turn was annotated when the interaction partner initiated a speaking turn or when the same speaker continued with a new turn following the completion of their previous TCU.
Short vocal response tokens were coded as vocal backchannels when they occurred either within the current speaker's turn or at a transition relevance place (TRP) (Gardner, 2001; Yngve, 1970).

text.text: Backchannels occurring at a TRP could be followed by a speaking turn produced by the same person.
As an exception, short responses to polar questions occurring at a TRP were coded as turns rather than backchannels, as they constituted answers to the preceding question.
When annotating the nods, the onset was coded manually from the perceived initiation of a vertical head movement, either downward or upward.
A nod was defined as a discrete vertical head movement including both a downward and an upward turn, in either order (Voutilainen et al., 2018).

text.text: CountVectorizer was configured to consider n-grams consisting of one to three words, thereby capturing both individual terms and short multi-word expressions. c-TF-IDF was then used to estimate the relative importance of these terms within each cluster, allowing the terms most representative of each identified topic to be extracted.
The model identified 244 distinct topics across the dataset and assigned each utterance to one of these topics.
Each utterance was linked to the 384-dimensional embedding representing that topic in the semantic space.
Each assignment was accompanied by a probability score indicating how strongly the utterance belonged to the assigned topic.
The resulting utterance-level data, including person-specific topic assignments and their probabilities, were exported as CSV files for further processing.
These data were subsequently used to derive two variables characterizing conversational content: topic exploration breadth and topic shift strength (see section 2.6.3).

Frames with missing values were linearly interpolated.

For gaze estimation, frames with low tracking confidence (≤ .80) or unsuccessful facial tracking were additionally treated as missing and interpolated, as gaze estimates become unreliable when facial features cannot be adequately tracked.

The resulting signals were low-pass filtered to attenuate high-frequency noise, using a second-order Butterworth filter with measure-specific cutoff frequencies (0.5 Hz for AU12 activity and 3 Hz for gaze direction).

Because smiling and gaze were examined as listener engagement behaviors, the preprocessed signals were restricted to non-speaking periods, defined as periods outside the onset-to-offset interval of each participant's own speaking turns (Figure 2, panel C).

text.text: Participants rated the extent to which each statement described them.

Each item corresponds to one of the five personality dimensions, for example: "Is talkative" (extraversion), "Tends to find fault with others" (agreeableness; reverse-coded), "Does a thorough job" (conscientiousness), "Is depressed" (neuroticism), and "Is original, comes up with new ideas" (openness).
Responses were given on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
Traits from both the participant and their dyadic partner were used to predict conversational outcomes in our analyses.
These traits are referred to as actor and partner traits in later sections.
Internal consistency for the trait scales was acceptable to high: openness (α = 0.74), conscientiousness (α = 0.80), extraversion (α = 0.85), agreeableness (α = 0.75), and neuroticism (α = 0.82).

Speech gap duration was calculated as the duration of the temporal gap (in seconds) between the offset of the partner's turn and the onset of the subject's response (a turn or a vocal backchannel response).
Positive values indicate a gap between turns and negative values reflect overlapping speech.
Only the cases where the response was associated with the partner's turn ending were used to calculate this metric, in order for it to reflect actual speaker transitions.
Extreme values exceeding ±2.5 standard deviations from the mean were removed.
Mean speech gap duration was then calculated for each participant across all valid speaker transitions within the conversation.
Turn length was calculated as the difference between turn onset and offset (in seconds) for every turn occurring within the first five minutes of conversation.
Mean turn length was then calculated as the subject-wise mean of this variable.
A Box-Cox transformation was applied (λ = -0.38) for statistical testing, after which the assumptions related to model residuals were deemed satisfactory.
The conversation content data with person-and utterance-specific topic assignments and their probabilities were used to derive topic exploration breadth and topic shift strength.
Both variables were calculated based on utterances with a BERTopic assignment probability of at least .20.
Of the 5,653 total utterances, 3,409 (60.3%) met this threshold.
By excluding low-probability utterances, we aimed to reduce the influence of uncertain and noisy topic assignments on the analyses.
Topic exploration breadth was calculated as the mean pairwise cosine distance across all unordered pairs of a participant's retained utterances, using the topic embedding assigned to each utterance.
Repeated assignments to the same topic were retained and therefore contributed zero-distance within-topic pairs.

Topic exploration breadth therefore reflects the overall semantic diversity of a participant's contributions across the conversation, with higher values indicating that their utterances spanned more semantically distinct topics and lower values indicating greater concentration within a narrower range of topics.
Topic shift strength was calculated across consecutive utterances produced by different speakers.
Speaker turns were first identified from the complete temporally ordered sequence of all utterances within each dyad, before applying the topic-probability threshold.
In most cases, a manually annotated turn contained a single utterance, although some turns comprised two or more utterances.

For each turn transition, the last utterance meeting the probability threshold in the immediately preceding partner speaker turn and the first utterance meeting the probability threshold in the current actor speaker turn were selected.
Thus, when the utterance closest to the speaker boundary did not meet the threshold, the nearest eligible utterance within the same speaker turn was used.
This procedure increased the number of usable transitions while retaining only utterances with sufficiently reliable topic assignments.

The cosine distance between the BERTopic topic embeddings assigned to the selected partner and actor utterances was then calculated, with the resulting value assigned to the speaker of the response utterance.
Cosine distances at transition points were then averaged separately for each participant.
Higher values therefore indicate that a participant's responses were, on average, more distant in topic space from the last partner utterance in the preceding speaker turn.
To improve the robustness of the participant-level estimates, participants with fewer than five valid turn transitions were omitted from analyses involving this variable, resulting in n = 136.
Vocal backchannels and nods occurring within the first five minutes of interaction were counted separately for each participant from the annotation output csv files.

To account for differences in listening time, these counts were standardized by dividing them by the participant's listening time (calculated by subtracting the total duration of the participant's turns from the five minutes of interaction time) and expressing them as backchannel rates (per minute).
Thus, these variables reflect how frequently participants produced nods and vocal backchannels when listening to the speech of their dyadic partner.
Since these instances were manually annotated by a research assistant, inter-rater reliability was assessed for both nods and vocal backchannels.
For this, two dyads were randomly sampled from each of the pools defined by gender, communication channel, and language group, resulting in 16 total dyads.
These dyads were then independently re-annotated by a second coder.
Each coder calculated the participant-level rates per minute over the 5-min conversation.
Agreement between coders was then estimated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs).
Inter-rater reliability was high for both nodding rate (ICC = .90, 95% CI [.81, .95]) and vocal backchannel rate (ICC = .94, 95% CI [.65, .98]).
Finally, in order to satisfy the residual-related assumptions of our statistical models, Box-Cox transformations were applied to vocal backchanneling rate (λ = 0.55) and nodding rate (λ = 0.30).

Smiling was operationalized using OpenFace estimates of Action Unit 12 (AU12; lip corner puller), which reflects activation of the zygomaticus major muscle and constitutes a core facial action underlying smiling (Ekman & Friesen, 1978; Rychlowska et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Smiling was operationalized using OpenFace estimates of Action Unit 12 (AU12; lip corner puller), which reflects activation of the zygomaticus major muscle and constitutes a core facial action underlying smiling <ref type="bibr">(Ekman & Friesen, 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rychlowska et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: To account for between-person differences in tonic AU12 activity, the preprocessed AU12 signal was mean-centered within participants and rectified such that values below the participant-specific baseline were set to zero.
Smiling was quantified as the mean of this signal across listener periods, with higher values indicating greater average smiling activity.
A Box-Cox transformation was applied to the resulting participant-level variable to satisfy the residual-related assumptions of the statistical models (λ = 0.63).
Gaze dispersion was operationalized using OpenFace estimates of horizontal (gaze_angle_x) and vertical (gaze_angle_y) gaze direction, expressed in radians.

For each participant, the standard deviations of the preprocessed horizontal and vertical gaze angles across listener periods were calculated separately and summed to obtain an overall gaze dispersion score.
Higher values indicated greater variation in gaze direction across the interaction, whereas lower values indicated more concentrated and stable gaze orientation.

As preliminary checks of the success of random assignment, we first examined whether participants in the two communication media differed in age or gender distribution.
We then tested whether personality trait scores differed between the communication media using linear models in which each personality trait was predicted by communication medium.
Having established the comparability of the two groups, we used the same modeling approach to examine the effects of communication medium on the eight conversational behaviors.

Here, behavioral variables were z-standardized; thus, the reported estimates (b) represent differences between the two communication media expressed in standard deviation units of the respective variable.

To account for potential dependence between dyad members, cluster-robust standard errors were calculated using dyad as the clustering variable, with CR2 correction and Satterthwaite-adjusted degrees of freedom.

For our main hypothesis tests, we examined whether the Big Five traits of both actor and partner predicted interactional behavior across three outcome clusters: turn-taking dynamics (average speech gap and turn duration), content development (topic exploration breadth, topic shift strength), and engagement signalling of the listener (vocal backchanneling, nodding, gaze, smiling).
First, each outcome was predicted by the main effects of actor and partner traits and the communication medium in an ordinary least squares regression framework.

To control for possible confounding effects of partner's turn count on backchanneling (since the amount of partner's turns was assumed to covary with the amount of listener backchanneling), it was included as a covariate in the models for nodding and vocal backchanneling.
The same cluster robust framework and the same data transformations for engagement variables were used for these models as in the previous step.
For the personality effects, p values were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg FDR procedure separately within each trait and each of the three outcome clusters.
Traits were treated as separate groupings in the FDR correction because the hypotheses concerned the effects of each personality trait independently.

Accordingly, the correction pool comprised four effects (actor and partner effects on two outcomes) for each trait in the turn-taking cluster, four effects for each trait in the content development cluster (actor and partner effects on two outcomes), and eight effects for each trait in the engagement-signalling cluster (actor and partner effects on four outcomes).
As secondary hypothesis tests (H2), we examined whether the effects of actor and partner personality traits on the outcome variables depended on communication medium.
For this purpose, we included communication medium-by-trait interaction terms alongside the corresponding main effects in the models.
The p-values from these secondary hypothesis tests were FDR-corrected separately from those of the primary analyses.
Correction was performed separately within each trait and outcome cluster, with the correction pools containing only the interaction terms.
Finally, as an exploratory analysis, we examined whether the effects of actor personality traits on the outcome variables depended on the partner's personality traits.
For this analysis, we included actor-by-partner interaction terms for each trait alongside the trait and communication-medium main effects.
Here, the FDR correction was not applied due to the exploratory nature of the analyses.
First, as a preliminary check, we examined whether the face-to-face and video-mediated groups differed in participant characteristics.
The groups did not differ significantly in age, t(147) = 0.23, p = .819, or gender distribution, χ²(1) = 0.39, p = .530.
Personality trait scores likewise did not differ significantly between the two communication medium groups (Table 2).

text.text: Together, these results indicated that the sampling procedure produced broadly comparable groups with respect to demographic characteristics and personality traits.
Differences in conversational behaviors between the communication mediums were examined.

Regarding turn-taking dynamics, we found shorter speech gaps in the face-to-face condition than in the video-mediated condition (b = -0.631, 95% CI [-0.931, -0.331], p < .001), indicating faster responses to partner's turn during face-to-face interactions.

There were also no significant differences in the variables related to conversation content between the two groups (ps ≥ .406).

Regarding the engagement signalling, we found less smiling (b = -0.516, 95% CI [-0.873, -0.159], p = .005) and more gaze dispersion (b = 0.753, 95% CI [0.454, 1.051], p < .001) in the face-to-face conversations compared to the video-mediated conversations, with no significant differences in vocal backchanneling or nodding (ps ≥ .070).

When testing the interaction effects between communication medium and partner and actor traits (H2), we found no effects that were significant even at the uncorrected level (ps ≥ .097), indicating that, contrary to H2, communication medium did not alter the effects of actor or partner personality traits on turn-taking dynamics (see Supplementary Table 1).

text.text: Finally, when exploring the trait-wise actor-partner interaction effects on speech gap duration, we found two significant interaction effects: a positive interaction effect between actor and partner openness (β = 0.131, 95% CI [0.005, 0.257], p = .043, p FDR = .144), and a negative interaction effect between actor and partner neuroticism (β = -0.147, 95% CI [-0.285, -0.008], p = .040, p FDR = .144).

The openness interaction indicated that partner's openness increased the positive effect of actor openness on speech gap duration, whereas the neuroticism interaction indicated that partner's neuroticism made the effect of actor neuroticism on speech gap duration more negative.

We also found a negative interaction effect between partner and actor extraversion on turn length (β = -0.174, 95% CI [-0.323, -0.024], p = .026, p FDR = .144), indicating that dyads with both partners having high extraversion produced shorter turns (see Supplementary table 2 for full results).

text.text: Higher actor extraversion was associated with more prominent vocal backchanneling (β = 0.221, 95% CI [0.076, 0.367], p = .004, p FDR = .015) and with smiling (β = 0.179, 95% CI [0.027, 0.331], p = .022, p FDR = .045).

So was partner extraversion positively associated with vocal backchanneling (β = 0.192, 95% CI [0.032, 0.353], p = .020, p FDR = .045) and smiling (β = 0.295, 95% CI [0.124, 0.465], p = .001, p FDR = .009).
Higher actor conscientiousness was associated with more frequent nodding (β = 0.244, 95% CI [0.086, 0.402], p = .003, p FDR = .027).
Five additional associations met the uncorrected significance threshold.

Actor openness was associated with less frequent vocal backchanneling (β = -0.142, 95% CI [-0.281, -0.004], p = .045, p FDR = .119), whereas actor extraversion was associated with more frequent nodding (β = 0.155, 95% CI [0.001, 0.310], p = .049, p FDR = .079).

Partner openness was associated with decreased smiling (β = -0.172, 95% CI [-0.322, -0.022], p = .026, p FDR = .103) and lower gaze dispersion (β = -0.212, 95% CI [-0.374, -0.050], p = .012, p FDR = .095), whereas partner agreeableness was associated with increased smiling (β = 0.182, 95% CI [0.029, 0.335], p = .021, p FDR = .170).
However, as these effects did not survive FDR correction, they should be interpreted with caution.

Additionally, we found a significant effect of communication medium on vocal backchanneling (b = 0.403, 95% CI [0.104, 0.701], p = .009), which was not present in the models that did not include personality traits as predictors.
This indicated more frequent predicted vocal backchanneling during face-to-face interaction than in video-mediated conversations when personality trait scores were at their mean level.

The present study examined how Big Five personality traits are associated with conversational behavior within a dyad and whether these associations depend on the communication medium.
Using a multimethod approach, we examined both actor and partner personality effects on turn-taking dynamics, conversational content, and listener engagement signaling during first encounters.
The findings provided partial support for H1, according to which different personality traits were expected to be associated with distinct patterns of conversational behavior.

Specifically, higher actor openness predicted longer speaking turns and longer gaps between turns but was negatively associated with engagement signaling and unrelated to content development, providing only partial support for H1.1.

Similarly, H1.2 concerning conscientiousness received partial support: higher actor conscientiousness was associated with more frequent nodding, but the hypothesized association with gaze orientation was not observed.
Unexpectedly, partner consciousness was associated with the actor's broader exploration of topics.
Extraversion emerged as the most consistent predictor of conversational behavior.
As hypothesized in H1.3, higher extraversion in both actors and partners was associated with shorter speech gaps.
Higher extraversion in both actors and partners was further associated with more frequent vocal backchanneling and with increased smiling.
The hypotheses concerning agreeableness (H1.4) and neuroticism (H1.5) received no clear support as none of these effects survived correction for multiple testing.
Exploratory analyses of actor-partner interactions further indicated that combinations of dyad members' openness, neuroticism, and extraversion were associated with turn-taking dynamics.
Finally, with regard to H2, the analyses provided no evidence that personality-behavior associations differed between face-to-face and video-mediated interactions.

Thus, although communication medium itself influenced several aspects of conversational behavior, there were no substantial personality-related differences in conversational behavior across the two interaction settings.
Together, these findings suggest that personality is expressed through distinct patterns of conversational behavior that generalize across face-to-face and video-mediated first encounters.
We next discuss these findings in more detail trait by trait, starting with those that showed the most robust effects.

Consistent with our hypotheses and with previous studieshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?nUPECu people with higher extraversion exhibited faster and more active conversational style (Cuperman & Ickes, 2009; Dewaele & Furnham, 1999; Wang & Ziano, 2022) , marked by rapid turn-taking and greater engagement signalling.

text.text: For turn-dynamics, the associations emerged for both actor and partner extraversion: actors higher in extraversion took the turn more rapidly, but actors also responded more rapidly when their partners were more extraverted.
This pattern highlights the fact that extraversion of both interlocutors contributes to the pace of conversational exchange.
The same energetic fast-pace style was present in engagement cueing.
Extraverted actors and people interacting with extraverted partners provided more vocal backchannels and smiled more.

Given that rapid turn transitions and active backchanneling as listeners are particularly important in defining interactional satisfaction during initial conversations (Itzchakov & Wheelerhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?XRukAk 2024; Kawana, 1986; Templeton et al., 2023) , the finding may help explain why extraverted individuals are particularly successful in forming new social ties and tend to develop larger social networks (Feiler & Kleinbaum, 2015; Rollings et al., 2023).

text.text: Openness, in contrast, was associated with an almost opposite conversational style.
People high in openness produced longer speaking turns and took longer to respond.
These outcomes are likely related to each other, as people inhale deeper in preparation for a longer response, thereby taking longer to initiate their response (Torreira et al., 2015).
text.formatted: These outcomes are likely related to each other, as people inhale deeper in preparation for a longer response, thereby taking longer to initiate their response <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Torreira et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: People with higher openness also displayed less engagement through vocal backchannels, and their partners smiled less and maintained more eye contact, although these engagement-related effects did not remain significant after correction for multiple testing.
The overall pattern was consistent with a slower-paced interactional style characterized by greater consideration and deliberation (Tannen, 1984).
text.formatted: The overall pattern was consistent with a slower-paced interactional style characterized by greater consideration and deliberation <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Tannen, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: This interpretation is compatible with the broader characterization of openness as involving greater intellectual engagement and receptiveness to complex or novel ideas (DeYoung, 2015; McCrae & Costa, 1997).
text.formatted: This interpretation is compatible with the broader characterization of openness as involving greater intellectual engagement and receptiveness to complex or novel ideas <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(DeYoung, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">McCrae & Costa, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: One exception to this pattern was that people high in openness did not explore the conversational topic space more broadly, contrary to our hypothesis.

The contrasting associations of extraversion and openness are nevertheless informative: whereas extraversion appears to manifest in fast-paced interpersonal exchange characterized by overt mutual engagement, openness appears to manifest in slower-paced, more deliberative actor turns resulting in less overt partner engagement.

Conscientiousness has received relatively little attention in previous research on conversational behavior, but the present findings suggest that it may nevertheless shape specific aspects of interaction.
In prior research utilizing the Parasocial Consensus Sampling approach, the trait was associated with more frequent nodding (Huang & Gratch, 2013).
text.formatted: In prior research utilizing the Parasocial Consensus Sampling approach, the trait was associated with more frequent nodding <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Huang & Gratch, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In the current study, this finding was replicated in naturalistic conversation, with actors higher in conscientiousness nodding more frequently.
Two additional partner effects provide an interesting perspective on how conscientiousness may influence the development of conversational content.
Interestingly, higher partner conscientiousness was associated with broader topic exploration by the actor but with smaller semantic shifts between consecutive utterances.
One possible explanation is that more conscientious individuals use what Mishler (1978) termed interrogative series to initiate and maintain conversational flow through successive questions.
text.formatted: One possible explanation is that more conscientious individuals use what <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Mishler (1978)</ref> termed interrogative series to initiate and maintain conversational flow through successive questions.

text.text: Such interrogative series could explain why partners covered a broader range of conversational topics while simultaneously showing smaller turn-to-turn semantic shifts: successive questions may elicit information across different topics, while partners' responses remain semantically closely related to the questions that elicited them.

These effects suggest that conscientiousness may shape conversation not only through individuals' own behavior but also through the way they scaffold the conversational contributions of their partners.
In regard to agreeableness and neuroticism, the effects were found to be surprisingly weak.

As prior research had associated high agreeableness with greater engagement signaling (Berry & Hansenhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?dntn75 2000; Cuperman & Ickes, 2009a; Funder & Sneed, 1993; Huang & Gratch, 2013) , we assumed this link to be found also in our data but none of the direct actor or partner effects reached significance.

text.text: This suggests that, at least during brief interactions between previously unacquainted individuals, the rapidity of conversational exchange or the expressions of engagement may be more strongly associated with the energetic and socially assertive tendencies characteristic of extraversion than with the cooperative and affiliative tendencies characteristic of agreeableness.
Based on prior research (Huang & Gratch, 2013), we also expected higher neuroticism to be associated with reduced engagement signaling through smiling and nodding.
text.formatted: Based on prior research <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Huang & Gratch, 2013)</ref>, we also expected higher neuroticism to be associated with reduced engagement signaling through smiling and nodding.

text.text: This hypothesis was, likewise, not supported by the data.

The only effects related to neuroticism came from the exploratory analyses of actor-partner interactions showing that gaps between speaker turns were shorter if both actor and partner were scoring high in neuroticism.

Together, these findings suggest that agreeableness and neuroticism have limited direct associations with conversational behavior during brief initial encounters, although neuroticism may become behaviorally relevant if both partners are high on the trait.
Turning to the communication medium, the current study revealed clear effects of video-calling on conversational behavior, replicating and extending previous evidence.

Compared with face-to-face interaction, video-mediated conversations were characterized by longer speech gaps and less frequent vocal backchanneling, consistent with previous findings (Boland et al., 2022; Brucks & Levav, 2022; Söderman et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Compared with face-to-face interaction, video-mediated conversations were characterized by longer speech gaps and less frequent vocal backchanneling, consistent with previous findings <ref type="bibr">(Boland et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Brucks & Levav, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Söderman et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, however, the effects of video calling on engagement signalling were not uniformly suppressive.

Participants smiled more frequently and maintained more direct gaze toward their partners during video-mediated than face-to-face interaction, suggesting that some visual engagement signals may be enhanced rather than diminished by the video-call setting (Croes et al., 2019;  see also Walther, 1992).

text.text: The most notable finding, however, was the consistency of personality-behavior associations across communication media.
Contrary to H2, none of the trait associations differed significantly between face-to-face and video-mediated interaction.

This is particularly noteworthy given previous evidence that video calling not only alters conversational dynamics (Boland et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?JA7iaZ 2022; Brucks & Levav, 2022) but can also attenuate individual or group differences in engagement behavior, such as culturally rooted variation in vocal backchanneling and nodding (Söderman et al., 2026) , and disrupt interpersonal emotional dynamics (Lepistö et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This is particularly noteworthy given previous evidence that video calling not only alters conversational dynamics <ref type="bibr">(Boland et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Brucks & Levav, 2022)</ref> but can also attenuate individual or group differences in engagement behavior, such as culturally rooted variation in vocal backchanneling and nodding <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Söderman et al., 2026)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?JA7iaZ">,</ref> and disrupt interpersonal emotional dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lepistö et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings therefore suggest that although video-mediated communication changes the overall level and timing of several conversational behaviors, we found no evidence that it alters how personality differences are expressed through these behaviors.
In this sense, personality-related patterns of conversational behavior appear to survive the technological transmission of first encounters.
The present findings should be interpreted in light of several features of the interactional setting.
Participants engaged in five-minute conversations with previously unacquainted same-sex partners, with the explicit goal of getting acquainted.

This standardized setting provided a controlled context for examining individual differences in conversational behavior and for comparing face-to-face and video-mediated interactions, but it also defines important boundary conditions for the generalizability of the findings.

First, the instructions to become acquainted, together with participants' knowledge of the limited time, may have restricted the range of topics discussed and the extent to which participants explored topics.

Consequently, the absence of other personality effects on topic development should not be interpreted as evidence that conscientiousness is the only trait related to conversational content more generally.

As conscientiousness is related to goal directed behavior (Wilmot & Oneshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?MDwDvj 2019) , merely giving participants the goal of getting acquainted might have brought out the observed effect.
text.formatted: As conscientiousness is related to goal directed behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Wilmot & Ones, 2019)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?MDwDvj">,</ref> merely giving participants the goal of getting acquainted might have brought out the observed effect.

text.text: Longer and more naturally unfolding conversations, in which participants can establish their own conversational goals, may therefore provide greater opportunities for personality differences to emerge.
Second, the sample consisted exclusively of same-sex dyads.
There is evidence showing that overt behavior such as eye contact and time spent talking is different in same-sex and different-sex dyads (e.g. Garcia et al., 1991; Mulac, 1989; Mulac et al., 1987).
text.formatted: There is evidence showing that overt behavior such as eye contact and time spent talking is different in same-sex and different-sex dyads (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Garcia et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Mulac, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Mulac et al., 1987)</ref>.

text.text: Different-sex dyads may thus involve distinct interactional dynamics that influence how personality is behaviorally expressed and how partners respond to one another.
Future research should directly compare same-sex and different-sex interactions to determine whether dyadic sex composition moderates the effects of personality traits on conversational behavior.
Third, the study only examined interactions between strangers.

This was useful for examining personality-related differences without the influence and complexity of an established relationship, but it also limits the extent to which the findings can be generalized to conversations in established relationships, such as between friends, colleagues, or romantic partners.
Familiarity may change both the topics that participants discuss and the interactional meanings and frequencies of behaviors such as pauses, nodding, and smiling.

For examplehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?EYpi0s it has been shown that friends explore broadening conversational topic spaces while strangers converge (Speer et al., 2024) , suggesting that personality too may manifest differently when participants already share interactional history.
text.formatted: For example, it has been shown that friends explore broadening conversational topic spaces while strangers converge <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Speer et al., 2024)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?EYpi0s">,</ref> suggesting that personality too may manifest differently when participants already share interactional history.

text.text: Future research should compare stranger and familiar-partner interactions to determine whether the observed personality-behavior associations are stable across relationship contexts.
Finally, although the present sample was relatively large for a dyadic interaction study, statistical power was limited for detecting small personality effects.

Sensitivity analyses indicated that the study had 80% power to detect standardized actor and partner effects of approximately β = .23-.28 and trait × medium interaction effects of β = .24-.28, depending on the trait and outcome.
Several of the observed personality effects were smaller than these values, suggesting that effects of comparable or smaller magnitude could have remained undetected.

This is particularly important when interpreting the results for H2: although the findings indicate that trait effects did not differ substantially between face-to-face and video-mediated interaction, smaller moderating effects of communication medium cannot be ruled out.
Larger dyadic samples will therefore be needed to determine whether the communication medium moderates some trait-behavior associations to a smaller degree.
Despite these boundary conditions, the present study provides a broad and methodologically rigorous examination of how personality is expressed in naturalistic conversational behavior.

By combining manually annotated turn-taking, computational analysis of conversational content, and computer vision measures of listener engagement with dyadic actor-partner analyses, the study moves beyond single behavioral indicators and examines personality expression across multiple interacting layers of conversation.

Empirically, the findings identify distinct conversational fingerprints associated particularly with extraversion, openness, and conscientiousness, while demonstrating that personality can shape not only individuals' own conversational behavior but also the behavior of their interaction partners.

Finally, the absence of substantial differences in personality-behavior associations between face-to-face and video-mediated interaction suggests that these interactional expressions of personality persist across rather different communication environments.

The present findings demonstrate that personality is expressed in distinct fingerprint patterns of conversational behavior that extend beyond individuals' own actions to the behavior of their partners.
Most notably, the findings point to different interactional modes through which conversational flow can be maintained.

Extraversion is associated with a fast-paced, highly responsive mode characterized by rapid turn transitions and active engagement signaling, whereas openness is associated with a slower and more deliberative mode characterized by longer speaking turns, longer response latencies, and less overt engagement signaling.

Conscientiousness, in turn, is associated with nodding and with partners' development of conversational content, illustrating how personality can shape not only one's own behavior but also the way one's partner is contributing to the encounter.
Thus, there may be actor and partner-linked fingerprint patterns of conversational behavior, rather than a single behavioral profile emerging from the actors' own personality traits.

Importantly, the absence of substantial differences in personality-behavior associations across face-to-face and video-mediated interaction suggests that interactional fingerprints of personality survive substantial changes in the technological conditions of communication.

Together, the findings provide an empirical and theoretical foundation for conceptualizing these fingerprints as a multimodal, dyadic phenomenon, shaped not only by individuals' own traits but also by those of their interaction partners.
